thesis: Dublin in May is when the city remembers that it has an outside and decides to use it.
scene: It's 6pm on a Thursday near the Grand Canal. A pub has moved its doors open and a crowd has formed on the pavement that was not there at five. Someone is holding a pint in both hands because there is nowhere to set it down. Two people who work together are standing with their coats over their arms, having brought them out of habit and not needed them. The light is coming in low from the west and will be doing this for another three hours. A man leans against the lamppost and it is understood that the lamppost is now part of the pub. Nobody has decided to leave. Nobody is going to.

sceneAnchors.text: The enclosed park in the center that fills on the first warm day and stays full until the last. In May the deck chairs come out. The lunchtime crowd is not eating lunch — they are lying in the sun on a Wednesday.

The long pier stretching into Dublin Bay where May brings the walkers out at dusk, in numbers that make it a procession rather than a walk. Couples. People with dogs. People on their own walking away from something and back to it. The turn at the end is where everyone stops for a moment without deciding to.

Where the Friday afternoon pint has moved outdoors and the path is lined with people who are technically still on the clock but clearly aren't. Nobody has a table and nobody appears to want one. The canal holds the last of the light for longer than the streets do, which is why the crowd thins from the road end first.

locals: Taking the pint outside as a reflex, not a decision — the door is open and that is the whole of the reasoning. Staying later than planned, which in May is every time. Making a walk into an evening, and then into a second pub further along the canal that somebody suggested without checking whether anyone wanted to go. Coats are carried rather than worn. There is a specific conversation that happens at about half eight, when somebody points out how bright it still is, and everybody agrees, and this happens most evenings for a month without anyone finding it repetitive.

localWord.translation: everything is fine, and more than fine
localWord.body: The Dublin unit of contentment. Not ecstatic, not disappointed — grand. When someone on the pier says it is a grand evening, they mean the city has delivered on something it owed them.

changes: The city expands. The same square footage as February but with the pavement counted as space, and the canal bank counted twice. The pub is inside and outside at once and no one is sure where the line is anymore. You stop thinking about where you will end the evening, because the evening has stopped having an end.
start: The evening walk. The pint on the pavement, taken standing because the sitting is all gone. The decision, at seven, that there is still enough light for one more thing — and being right, which is the part that keeps happening. You start leaving the coat. You start saying you will walk it, meaning forty minutes along the canal, and finding that somebody else is walking the same way.
stop: The indoor default. May in Dublin is when people stop assuming the plan ends inside, and the assumption goes quietly, without anyone announcing the change. You stop booking a table for a thing that turns out to be a pavement. You stop treating a clear evening as something to be used carefully, because there is another one tomorrow.
returns: The long evening. The version of a day where nine is still daytime and the light tells you there is time, which after an Irish winter is not a small thing to be handed back. Nothing is being celebrated and nothing has been arranged. The doors are simply open and the pavement is full and it will be like this tomorrow.
remember: By May Dublin has remembered it is a coastal city. You will remember too.

items.label: February
items.body: The pubs are full and the outside is not an option.

items.label: May
items.body: The doors come open and the city spills out.

items.label: August
items.body: The sun is still there but the tourists have arrived and the pavement is shared.
